elements.element: The aggregate liability cap applies mutually to both parties.
elements.evidence: Section 9.1(c) caps IBM's liability and the parallel Section 9.2(c) caps Customer's liability at the same measure ("the greater of $100,000 or the charges paid by Customer to IBM for the Services in the twelve (12) months immediately preceding the accrual of the first claim"); the new carve-out sentence expressly references both 9.1(c) and 9.2(c), preserving symmetry.

elements.element: The cap is the greater of fees paid or payable in the 12 months preceding the claim and USD 1,000,000.
elements.evidence: Retained cap is "the greater of $100,000 or the charges paid ... in the twelve (12) months immediately preceding the accrual of the first claim" — the floor is USD 100,000 rather than USD 1,000,000, and the basis is charges "paid" only, not "paid or payable". Redline does not touch the cap amount or basis.

elements.element: The exclusion of indirect and consequential damages applies mutually to both parties.
elements.evidence: Section 10.a: "In no event will either party be liable to the other for special, incidental, or indirect damages or for any consequential damages (including lost profits or savings)" — bilateral on its face; the proviso only preserves Customer's payment obligations.

elements.element: Breach of confidentiality obligations is uncapped.
elements.evidence: New Subsection d: "The limitations in Subsections 9.1(c) and 9.2(c) do not apply to damages arising from a party's breach of its confidentiality obligations...". Because the carve-out sits inside Section 9, the Section 6 priority sentence ("the provisions of Sections 5, 9, and 10 herein will prevail") now carries the carve-out rather than defeating it.

elements.element: Breach of data protection and security obligations is uncapped.
elements.evidence: The added sentence lists only confidentiality, gross negligence and willful misconduct; no data protection or security carve-out appears anywhere in Sections 9 or 10, so security/data-protection breaches remain inside the 9.1(c)/9.2(c) cap.

Sections 9.1(a)/9.2(a) list "indemnification payments as provided in Section 8.1 / 8.2" as a separate liability category; the monetary limit in subsection (c) attaches only to "any other actual direct damages", so indemnification payments carry no monetary ceiling.
New Subsection d excludes "damages arising from ... its gross negligence" from the 9.1(c) and 9.2(c) limitations, mutually.
New Subsection d excludes "damages arising from ... its willful misconduct" from the 9.1(c) and 9.2(c) limitations, mutually.
No fraud carve-out in the added sentence or elsewhere in Sections 9/10; fraud damages remain subject to the 9.1(c)/9.2(c) cap.

elements.element: Infringement of the other party's intellectual property is uncapped.
elements.evidence: No IP-infringement carve-out was added; only indemnification payments under Sections 8.1/8.2 escape the monetary limit, which does not equate to a general carve-out for infringement of the other party's IP.

elements.element: Customer payment obligations are excluded from damages subject to the cap.
elements.evidence: Section 10.a's proviso only disapplies the consequential-damages exclusion to Customer's failure to pay; nothing states that Customer's payment obligations are not "damages" for purposes of the Section 9.2(c) cap, so unpaid charges above the cap arguably remain limited.

elements.element: The aggregate liability cap applies mutually to both parties.
elements.evidence: Mirror caps in 9.1(c) (IBM, its Affiliates and Subcontractors) and 9.2(c) (Customer and its Affiliates) at the identical measure; no unlimited-Customer-liability language remains.

elements.element: The cap is based on 12 months of fees.
elements.evidence: "the greater of $100,000 or the charges paid by Customer to IBM for the Services in the twelve (12) months immediately preceding the accrual of the first claim related to the Services" — a 12-month fee basis with a fixed floor; the "Services" charges are the substantive commercial fees, not an illusory narrow fee subset.
Sections 9.1(a)/9.2(a) carry indemnification payments as a stand-alone category outside the subsection (c) monetary ceiling, which applies only to "any other actual direct damages".

elements.element: Breach of confidentiality obligations is uncapped.
elements.evidence: Inserted Subsection d disapplies the 9.1(c)/9.2(c) limits to "damages arising from a party's breach of its confidentiality obligations", bilaterally; the Section 6 precedence clause makes Section 9 (as amended) controlling, so the carve-out is not contradicted.
Inserted Subsection d: limits "do not apply to damages arising from ... its gross negligence".
Inserted Subsection d: limits "do not apply to damages arising from ... its willful misconduct".

reasons: Fallback is position-complete: the mutual cap and 12-month fee basis already existed in Sections 9.1(c)/9.2(c), indemnification payments already sat outside the monetary ceiling under 9.1(a)/9.2(a), and the single inserted sentence supplies the three missing carve-outs (confidentiality, gross negligence, willful misconduct) mutually and unconditionally.

Preferred is not met: the floor remains USD 100,000 rather than USD 1,000,000, the basis is charges "paid" not "paid or payable", and there are no carve-outs for data protection/security, fraud, or infringement of the other party's IP, nor any statement that Customer's payment obligations are not damages subject to the cap. To reach preferred the drafter would need to amend the 9.1(c)/9.2(c) formula and extend the carve-out list.

Minimality holds: one carve-out sentence keyed by cross-reference to the two existing cap subsections, no rewrite of the caps, no survival tail, no added procedures, damages categories, or extras beyond the three fallback carve-outs; existing Customer-favourable language (Section 10 proviso, the separate indemnification category) is retained untouched.

Intent is preserved: the inserted subsection uses live cross-references to Subsections 9.1(c) and 9.2(c), leaves no undefined term, and does not conflict with the Section 6 precedence sentence — because the carve-out sits within Section 9, Section 6 now propagates rather than defeats it. Section 10's consequential-damages exclusion and its payment-obligation proviso are unaffected.

Classification as a deviation was correct pre-redline: the original text failed the fallback on confidentiality, gross negligence and willful misconduct carve-outs; the caps themselves sat at fallback and were properly left alone, with the preferred-level gaps noted in the comment rather than redlined.
